title: Profit & Loss
shortDescription: CP is what you paid, SP is what you got — every profit/loss percentage is measured against CP, and discount is measured against MP, never confuse the two bases.
genZNote: CP is what you paid, SP is what you got. Everything else is just the drama between them — and that drama is always measured against CP, not SP.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Profit % = ((SP−CP)/CP) × 100. Loss % = ((CP−SP)/CP) × 100. The single fact that resolves most Profit & Loss confusion: profit or loss percentage is ALWAYS relative to Cost Price (CP), never to Selling Price (SP), even though SP is the more recently mentioned number in most problem statements.

sections.heading: Marked Price → Discount → Selling Price
sections.body: Marked Price (MP) is the labelled/listed price. A discount percentage is applied to MP to get SP: SP = MP × (1 − Discount%/100). Profit/Loss is then calculated on THAT resulting SP against CP — discount and profit are two separate calculations on two different base quantities (MP for discount, CP for profit) chained together.

sections.heading: Worked Example — Standard vs Fast Method

steps.name: Standard method
steps.explanation: An item marked at ₹500 is sold at a 20% discount; CP was ₹350. SP = 500 × 0.80 = 400. Profit% = ((400−350)/350) × 100 ≈ 14.29%.
steps.purpose: Direct two-step application: discount first, profit second.

steps.name: Fast method for round numbers
steps.explanation: Once SP=400 is found via the ×0.8 shortcut (10% shortcut used twice, or 20% = ⅕ subtracted once), the profit fraction 50/350 = 1/7 ≈ 14.3% is faster to read off than a full percentage multiplication.
steps.purpose: Converts the final step into a simple fraction rather than a decimal percentage calculation.

sections.heading: Successive Discounts
sections.body: Two successive discounts (e.g. 10% then 5%) do NOT simply add to 15% — they combine the same way as successive percentage changes: net discount = d1 + d2 − (d1×d2)/100. For 10% then 5%: 10 + 5 − 0.5 = 14.5%, not 15%.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Calculating profit/loss percentage on SP instead of CP — always CP is the base.
Treating MP and CP as the same base — discount is off MP, profit/loss is off CP; mixing them gives the wrong SP or profit figure.
Adding two successive discount percentages directly instead of using the successive-change formula.
Assuming 'no profit no loss' means SP=0 — it means SP=CP.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Before touching a formula, write down which quantity is CP, which is MP, and which is SP — most errors come from mixing these up under time pressure, not from arithmetic mistakes.
For successive discounts, use d1+d2−(d1d2/100) directly rather than applying each discount as a separate multiplication step when only the net % is asked.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Profit/Loss % is always calculated relative to Cost Price; discount is calculated relative to Marked Price — these are two separate bases chained together.
keyFacts: Successive discounts combine as d1+d2−(d1×d2)/100, not by simple addition.
No profit no loss means SP = CP, not SP = 0.
commonConfusion: Discount is off MP; profit/loss % is off CP — two different reference points in the same problem.

highYieldFacts: Profit/Loss % base is always CP, never SP.
Successive discounts use the same non-additive combination formula as successive percentage changes.
commonTraps: Computing profit % on SP instead of CP.
mustRemember: SP = MP × (1 − Discount%/100), then Profit% is calculated on THAT SP against CP — two chained steps, two different bases.
